title: Good Pope John (1958–1963)
hookLine: a farmer's son, warm and brave, whose letter on peace was addressed to all people of goodwill

lines: A LETTER WITH A WIDE ADDRESS.
cards: A letter from a pope usually opens by saying who it is for. The bishops. The clergy.
The faithful. This one does all that, and then it keeps going: to all men of good will. Not only Catholics.
Not only believers. Anyone who means well, wherever they are.

The man who signed it grew up in a farming family in the hills of northern Italy, and he never lost the manner of a country priest: jokes, plain talk, a big laugh. People in Rome gave him a plainer name. Good Pope John.

teach.b: His name was Angelo Roncalli; as pope he took the name John. Start with the farm.

He came from a family that worked the land, and he wrote about that childhood with affection in his spiritual diary, later published as Journal of a Soul. He never pretended to be grander than he was. Then the window.

teach.h: HE OPENS A WINDOW: A COUNCIL.
teach.b: He surprised the Church by calling a council, a gathering of the world's bishops in Rome: the Second Vatican Council. Tradition says he described it as opening a window to let in fresh air.
What it changed in ordinary parishes is tomorrow's story. Then the letter. As pope he wrote an encyclical called Pacem in Terris, Latin for peace on earth.

teach.h: PEACE ON TRUTH, JUSTICE, LOVE, FREEDOM.
teach.b: Peace among nations, it says, has to stand on four things: truth, justice, love and freedom.

It speaks of the rights every human being has simply by being human, and the duties that come with them. And it was addressed not only to Catholics but to all people of good will. That phrase has an old sound.

teach.h: ON EARTH PEACE TO MEN OF GOOD WILL.
teach.b: On the night of Christ's birth, Luke's Gospel says, the angels sang, in the Douay-Rheims: "Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will."
A pope borrowed the angels' address for a letter about peace: the work of peace is shared with anyone willing to do it.

how: Catholics remember Saint John XXIII on his feast day, and Pacem in Terris is still read in Catholic schools, parishes and peace groups as a foundation of the Church's teaching on peace and human rights.

games.q: you're Pope John, writing a letter about peace in a tense world. who do you address it to?
games.why: after the bishops and the faithful, he added all people of good will, borrowing the angels' address from Luke.

practice: Bring to mind one person of goodwill, maybe someone you disagree with about a lot, but whose good intentions you trust: a neighbor, a coworker, a relative across a political line.
Let one honest sentence for them form, thank you, or I see what you're trying to do. If you pray, pray the angels' line from Luke for them; if not, simply wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Angelo Roncalli. The farmer's son who became pope, took the name John, called the Second Vatican Council, and wrote Pacem in Terris to all people of good will.

orig.note: Latin: peace on earth, the opening words that give the encyclical its name.

carryVoice: Your line: all people of goodwill. The week ran from Titus Brandsma and Irena Sendler through Dorothy Day, Peter Maurin, Gianna Beretta Molla and Pier Giorgio Frassati, to Good Pope John. See you tomorrow.
